title: Offset Cancellation
intro: Making devices larger to lower the offset costs capacitance, and packaging stress can shift offsets after test. Precision circuits instead measure their own offset in a dedicated clock phase, store it on capacitors, and subtract it. The same trick removes low-frequency noise (Razavi, Sections 14.2.2 and 14.2.3).

blocks.text: Threshold mismatch trades directly with gate capacitance: in an older 0.6 µm process, about 300 fF of channel capacitance per device for 1 mV of $V_{TH}$ mismatch. When many comparators hang on one input (as in a flash ADC), that load is prohibitive. Electronic cancellation sidesteps the trade, and as a bonus suppresses $1/f$ noise. The stored correction leaks away through junction and subthreshold currents, so it must be refreshed, typically at least every few hundred microseconds (a few kilohertz).

Put capacitors $C_1$, $C_2$ in series with the amplifier's outputs. In the cancellation phase short the inputs together (to a CM level) and short the far ends of the capacitors to a CM level too: the amplified offset $A_vV_{OS}$ ends up stored across the capacitors. In amplification the stored voltage subtracts exactly the offset, and the switches' charge-injection mismatch is the only residue. Because $A_vV_{OS}$ must not saturate the output, the gain is kept low, roughly below 10.

blocks.alt: Schematic. Differential inputs pass through switches to the left plates of capacitors C1 and C2; switches S1 and S2 can tie those plates to VCM. The right plates, nodes X and Y, drive the + and minus inputs of a fully differential amplifier Av. Switch S3 connects the amplifier's minus output back to X and S4 connects its plus output back to Y.
blocks.caption: Cancellation phase: S1 to S4 closed. The amplifier in unity feedback writes its own offset onto $C_1$ and $C_2$.

blocks.text: For high-gain amplifiers, put the capacitors at the inputs and close the amplifier in unity feedback during cancellation. Then

is stored across $C_1$, $C_2$. After the switches open, a zero input gives an output of $V_{OS}$, so the residual input-referred offset is $V_{OS}/A_v$, provided S3 and S4 inject equal charges and the amplifier's input capacitance is small compared with $C_1$, $C_2$. Unequal injection from S3 and S4 appears as an input offset, and with a large $A_v$ it can saturate the output.
Both storage methods put capacitors in the signal path. Their bottom-plate parasitics add poles (hurting phase margin in a feedback system) and slow settling, worsening the speed-power trade-off.

Keep the capacitors out of the signal path: an auxiliary amplifier $A_{aux}$ amplifies a voltage $V_1$ stored on $C_1$, $C_2$ and subtracts the result from the main amplifier's output. If $A_{aux}V_1 = A_1V_{OS1}$ the offset vanishes. $V_1$ is produced in a cancellation phase by closing a loop through a following stage and $A_{aux}$. In practice both are transconductors summing currents into a shared load $R$ (a folded-cascode op amp, with the correction $G_{m2}$ injecting current at the low-impedance folding nodes). Including the offset $V_{OS2}$ of $G_{m2}$:

When S3 and S4 open, a differential injection error $\Delta V$ on the storage capacitors is not corrected (the loop is open) and appears at the input as $(G_{m2}/G_{m1})\Delta V$, which is why $G_{m2}$ is made about $0.1G_{m1}$. The unity-gain sampler and multiply-by-two SC circuits cancel the op amp's offset in the same way (unless an equalising switch is added).

Offset is noise at zero frequency, so cancelling it right before use also cancels slowly varying noise. If the offset is stored at $t_1$ and the signal is sampled at $t_2 = t_1 + \Delta t$, only noise components fast enough to change appreciably in $\Delta t$ survive. A sinusoid of amplitude $A$ and frequency $f$ changes by at most $2\pi fA\Delta t$ in that time, so components well below $1/\Delta t$ are suppressed. This is correlated double sampling (CDS), first used in CCD imagers, and it is a strong weapon against MOS $1/f$ noise, whose corner can be 500 kHz to 1 MHz. Its price is aliasing: the sampling folds wideband noise down into the band.

blocks.title: Output storage limit
blocks.text: An amplifier with $A_v = 8$ has a 5 mV offset and an output range of ±0.5 V. What voltage is stored in output offset storage, and what is the largest gain that keeps the stored value below 10% of the range for offsets up to 10 mV?

blocks.title: Input storage residue
blocks.text: An amplifier with $A_v = 1000$ and $V_{OS} = 5$ mV uses input offset storage with $C_1 = C_2 = 1$ pF. What is the ideal residual offset? If S3 and S4 inject charges differing by 1 fC, what is the error?
solution: Injection mismatch: $1\text{ fC}/1\text{ pF} = 1$ mV, directly at the input: it dominates by a factor of 200.
blocks.answer: 5 µV ideally; about 1 mV with the injection mismatch.

blocks.title: Auxiliary-amplifier cancellation
blocks.text: $G_{m1}R = 1000$, $G_{m2} = 0.1G_{m1}$, and both stages have 5 mV offsets. Find the residual offset, and the error from a 1 mV injection mismatch.
blocks.answer: About 54 µV, plus 100 µV from injection.

blocks.title: How much does CDS help?
blocks.text: Samples are taken 20 ns after offset storage. Estimate the largest fractional change of a 100 kHz and of a 10 MHz noise component in that interval.
solution: $2\pi f\Delta t$: at 100 kHz, $2\pi \times 10^5 \times 2\times 10^{-8} = 0.013$ (1.3%), so it is almost entirely cancelled.
At 10 MHz the bound is 1.26, i.e. no suppression at all.
